about: The contradiction ledger (board 061), kept by factcheck@php.newsroom. One record per measure the reporting disagrees about. Every 'says' is verbatim from the capture or fetch named; 'sources' are vault slugs in the site's manifest; 'outside' are URLs not captured into the vault, never cited until captured. Status: open (the desk cannot yet say why they differ, or the site states one side as fact), explained (the desk can say why they differ, and the site should say it too), resolved (a later source settles it).

contradictions.measure: How much of the web: 70% of websites, or 70% of the Internet?

statements.says: a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world
statements.measures: share of websites using PHP

statements.says: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
statements.measures: the same figure, restated as a share of the Internet

statements.says: cyber-security firm Wiz estimating that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure
statements.measures: the Wiz figure, quoted with a word ('roughly') that is not in Wiz's post

statements.says: Websites shut down globally after AI finds a critical flaw affecting 70% of the internet
statements.measures: headline: share of the Internet; its own body says 'powers 70% of all websites'

contradictions.reading: One origin, Wiz, restated: a share of websites using PHP became a share of 'the Internet' affected, inside Wiz's own post. Every outlet in the vault that carries the figure traces to Wiz, so it is one source, not several (restates, not corroborates). None of them says how the 70% was measured; it matches the usual web-technology survey figure for sites whose server-side language is known, which is a share of websites, not of hosts, traffic or 'the Internet', and not a count of vulnerable installations. The BBC's 'roughly 70%' puts a word in Wiz's mouth that its post does not use. Run 3 (24 October): the investigation php-share traces 127 statements of the share in the vault to their origin and measures them against W3Techs, the HTTP Archive, BuiltWith and the scanners; it is on /factcheck/investigations/php-share/.
contradictions.settle: The survey Wiz relied on, captured, with its population and method.

statements.who: Amazon Threat Intelligence (CJ Moses, AWS Security Blog)
statements.says: we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.
statements.measures: exploitation attempts against Amazon's MadPot honeypot sensors, from 17 October and in volume from 21 October 02:00 UTC

statements.says: While CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication
statements.measures: exploitation observed by CISA, as of the alert's publication

statements.who: CISA ADP (SSVC in both CVE records)
statements.says: Exploitation: none
statements.measures: CISA's SSVC exploitation decision point at the time it was scored; unchanged in the records fetched 2026-10-22 18:27 UTC

statements.says: Neither CVE-2026-109618 nor CVE-2026-109619 is in the catalog's 1,754 entries.
statements.measures: CISA's official list of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation

statements.says: Officials in Germany, the Netherlands and Japan say they have not seen one succeed.
statements.measures: successful exploitation, as seen by national officials

statements.who: Amazon (the same AWS Security Blog post, as revised)
statements.says: PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.
statements.measures: Amazon's own revision of 'is now being broadly exploited in the wild', with no note; captured in the vault on 23 October (capture 20261023T160435Z)

statements.says: Sophos said its customer data showed scanning and a small number of failed exploit attempts.
statements.measures: Sophos's own success claim, withdrawn

statements.who: watchTowr (its own intel page and FAQ)
statements.says: watchTowr has observed exploitation in the wild through its Attacker Eye honeypot network.
statements.measures: honeypot traffic, listed by watchTowr as 'EXPLOITED IN THE WILD: Yes'

contradictions.reading: They measure different things at different times. Amazon counts attempts against its own sensors and honeypots; CISA and KEV record exploitation it has evidence of against real systems. Both can be true at once: attempts in volume, and no confirmed compromise of a named organisation. The site should never write 'exploited' without saying which of the two it means. Amazon's 'broadly exploited' is the stronger word, sourced to Amazon's own post in the vault; a KEV entry would be the first official signal that attempts have become compromises. Run 3 (24 October): Amazon itself has since narrowed its sentence from 'broadly exploited' to 'broad exploitation attempts', without a note: the strongest word on the exploitation side now agrees with the officials' reading. Run 5 (24 October): Sophos withdrew its earlier success claim at 21:21 UTC on 22 October, the same evening Amazon narrowed its wording: both strongest 'exploited' statements were walked back to attempts.
contradictions.settle: A KEV entry for either CVE, or a named organisation confirming a compromise.

statements.says: The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later
statements.measures: affected versions

statements.says: affected: 8.2 before 8.2.35, 8.3 before 8.3.36, 8.4 before 8.4.27, 8.5 before 8.5.12
statements.measures: the supported branches that received a fixed release

statements.says: the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1
statements.measures: the branches that got a source backport

statements.says: cpe:2.3:a:php:php, versionEndExcluding 8.2.35, with no starting version
statements.measures: NVD encodes every version before 8.2.35 as vulnerable

statements.who: CrowdStrike (blog), relayed to oss-security by Greenbone
statements.says: The specific HashTable ordering behind CVE-2026-109618 was introduced by a performance optimization in October 2017 and first shipped in PHP 7.3.0 (December 2018).
statements.measures: when each flaw's code path entered PHP: CVE-2026-109618 from 7.3.0; CVE-2026-109619's paths from 7.1 (serialization) and 5.4 (session)

contradictions.reading: Affected, supported and patched are three different lists. The CVE record lists only the supported branches the PHP project fixed; the backports reach down to 7.4; Cloudflare and NVD describe what is vulnerable, which goes back further. They are compatible, but read as a contradiction unless the site says so where it shows the version table. Run 4 (24 October): CrowdStrike gives each flaw its own start: CVE-2026-109618 from PHP 7.3.0, CVE-2026-109619 back to 5.4 through the session path. If it holds, 'every version since 5.4' is true only of the second flaw. CrowdStrike's own page also says both are in 'every PHP release from the 7.x and 8.x series', which its next sentence contradicts for 7.0 to 7.2. Not captured; the PHP project has not said.
contradictions.settle: The PHP project stating the earliest affected version.

contradictions.measure: How many systems are still unpatched?

statements.says: Out of 2.58 million internet-facing hosts seen on October 21, roughly 1.58 million were reporting identifiable PHP versions, and approximately 1.57 million were not patched
statements.measures: unpatched hosts among those whose PHP version is visible, on release day

statements.who: VulnCheck, VirusTotal and Censys, via SecurityWeek
statements.says: more than 1 million PHP servers were running unpatched software releases as of October 21
statements.measures: a floor, with no method given

statements.says: Major providers have implemented a fix, but globally 90% of systems at risk are yet to do so, researchers say.
statements.measures: unknown population and method

contradictions.reading: The site's claim reads as 1.57 million unpatched out of about 2.6 million hosts (about 60%). The source says 1.57 million out of the 1.58 million whose version could be read (about 99%, on the day the fix shipped); the 2.58 million is all hosts seen, most of which do not announce a version. The two framings give very different pictures. The BBC's 90% has no named counter or method and is not captured. Open, because the site states one framing as fact. Run 3 (24 October): the site now states both counters and Censys's denominator, so the framing difference is explained on the page; the BBC's 90% stays uncaptured.
contradictions.settle: Censys's own post (the vault notes say it was not found), or a later Censys count with the same population.

contradictions.measure: How many UK government services went down?

statements.who: The BBC live page, reporting a UK minister
statements.says: In the UK, a minister said just after midday that 32 government services were unavailable and four partially unavailable because they were being fixed
statements.measures: central government services, at one moment

statements.says: dozens of UK government services
statements.measures: unspecified; seen in the coverage review session, not fetched or captured by this desk
outside: The Register follow-up, URL not recorded in the coverage review

contradictions.reading: Probably the same count, described loosely by The Register. The BBC's line is verified in a fetch by this desk; it says 'a minister' without naming one or the House, so the coverage review's 'in the House of Lords' is not yet carried by any source this desk has read. Neither is captured into the vault: this record is a request to capture.
contradictions.settle: The Hansard record of the minister's answer, captured.

contradictions.measure: How many sites were taken offline?

statements.says: 10 operators offline
statements.measures: operators with a captured source in the exported manifest

statements.says: 50 sites in sites.csv, 2 of them with no back-up time
statements.measures: sites first reported dark by any public source, aggregators included, with dark and back-up times

statements.says: 40 sources not exported to this site, among them captures of Edinburgh council, French prefectures, ANTS, UNIGE, EPFL, Wikimedia status, and reports from Reuters, The Record and Global News
statements.measures: captured but not yet on the site

contradictions.reading: Breadth of collection, and an export lag. The site requires a captured source per row; the tracker accepts aggregator reports and says so per row. Part of the gap is not collection at all: the vault already holds captures of more offline operators than the site shows, because the site's export stopped at 144 sources.
contradictions.settle: Re-run the vault export; capture the tracker's sites.csv into the source watch on a schedule.

statements.who: Social posts relayed during the leak
statements.says: a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2)
statements.measures: a leaked number, corrected by the PHP Foundation

statements.says: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N, base score 9.2
statements.measures: CVSS version 4.0, scored by the vendor

statements.says: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, base score 9.8
statements.measures: CVSS version 3.1, scored by NIST, which rates attack complexity low where the vendor rated it high

contradictions.reading: 10.0 was wrong. 9.2 and 9.8 are both right, on two different scales scored by two different parties, and they disagree on one input: the vendor says attack complexity is high, NIST says low. The site explains 10.0 against 9.2 but never mentions 9.8, which is what a reader checking NVD, or a scanner reporting CVSS 3.1, will see.
contradictions.settle: Already settled as a reading; the site should carry the 9.8 and say what differs.

contradictions.measure: Which flaw was shown to give code execution on PHP-FPM?

statements.says: Remote code execution was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths
statements.measures: placed under CVE-2026-109618 in the post

statements.says: no complete FPM exploit has been demonstrated for this SAPI
statements.measures: CVE-2026-109618 on FPM

statements.says: It works with a normal dynamic FPM pool, although it depends on a suitable application operation.
statements.measures: CVE-2026-109619 on FPM

contradictions.reading: The advisories, written by the PHP security team per CVE, put the demonstrated FPM exploit under CVE-2026-109619, and say none was demonstrated for CVE-2026-109618. The Foundation's blog places FPM confirmation under CVE-2026-109618. The blog appears to have swapped the attribution. That RCE was shown on FPM is not in doubt; which flaw does it is.
contradictions.settle: A correction to the Foundation's post, or a PHP security team statement.

contradictions.measure: Did any technical detail leak on 20 October?

statements.says: They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked.
statements.measures: what circulated with the CVE IDs

statements.who: Daubois (a member of the PHP security team, own blog)
statements.says: A screenshot of the PHP2Shell tool, credited to Calif.IO, leaked alongside the advisory, and a short exploitation video went up and came down
statements.measures: a tool screenshot and a video

statements.says: details about the CVE identifiers and a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit leaked ahead of time
statements.measures: claims a PoC leaked

statements.says: Sansec cites a leaked screenshot of an exploit tool named PHP2Shell, whose banner claims the tool works against PHP 5.4.0 and later.
statements.measures: a screenshot of a tool banner

statements.says: At that point, no technical details leaked.
statements.measures: the Foundation's statement, with the time it applies to

statements.says: The CVE IDs leaked the day before, and Calif accidentally posted an exploit video that evening.
statements.measures: the order of events on 20 October

contradictions.reading: Probably different meanings of 'technical detail'. A screenshot of a tool banner and a demonstration video show that an exploit exists, not how it works; the Foundation may mean that no root cause or code leaked. The Hacker News's 'proof-of-concept exploit leaked' is stronger than anything else in the vault carries, and no capture shows a leaked PoC. Open until the Foundation or Daubois says what the Foundation meant. Run 3 (24 October), a fresh look with 112 more sources in the vault: the difference is time. The Foundation's 'no technical details leaked' describes the CVE IDs circulating from about 15:00 UTC on 20 October; The Register's report of it says 'At that point'. Calif's exploit video went up 'that evening' (Feross; Daubois; Wikipedia), after the pre-announcement. A video and a tool banner show that an exploit exists, not how it works; no capture shows leaked exploit code, so The Hacker News's 'proof-of-concept exploit leaked' most likely means the video. Both statements hold, each at its own time; a page that quotes the Foundation should keep its time.
contradictions.settle: A capture of the leaked screenshot or video, or the Foundation saying what 'technical details' covers.

contradictions.measure: When was the release planned, and when did it ship?

statements.says: It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC.
statements.measures: the planned times

statements.says: Originally scheduled for coordinated disclosure on October 22, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. UTC
statements.measures: the original plan, probably from the Foundation

statements.says: The disclosure was originally under embargo until Thursday 22 October at 11:00 ET; after the leak, PHP scheduled its release for 21 October
statements.measures: the original embargo, 15:00 UTC, attributed by others to watchTowr
the date the ChangeLog gives all four releases, which shipped on 21 October

statements.says: candidate pull requests under a private security branch scheduled for public disclosure on October 24.
statements.measures: a third planned date, 24 October, given with no source; no other statement in the vault gives it

contradictions.reading: The original embargo time has two values, 14:00 UTC (the Foundation, echoed by The Hacker News) and 11:00 ET, which is 15:00 UTC (watchTowr, echoed by CybelAngel and others). The release itself is stamped 13:34 UTC on the GitHub advisories, ahead of the announced 14:00. The ChangeLog still carries the original date. The site should say 'about 14:00 UTC, advisories at 13:34' and give both original times. Run 7: Lorikeet's blog gives a third planned date, 24 October, unsourced and alone in the vault (in its captures of 22 and 25 October); it does not change the reading.
contradictions.settle: A PHP project statement of the embargo time, or the pre-announcement's original text.

contradictions.measure: Is the fix in PHP 8.5.12 incomplete?

statements.who: Aaron Rainbolt on oss-security, relaying a Fediverse post
statements.says: the Fediverse is reporting that the fix to at least PHP 8.5.12 may be incomplete
statements.measures: an unconfirmed report from an unnamed person, relayed

statements.who: The same, relaying Canonical via a Matrix channel
statements.says: was told that it's "unrelated and not a real issue"
statements.measures: PHP's answer to Canonical, second-hand

statements.who: Jakub Zelenka, PHP security team, on oss-security (post 2026/10/22/15)
statements.says: This is unrelated issue with minimal impact (crash in one component in slightly unlikely scenario). It has nothing to do with the RCE.
statements.measures: PHP's own public answer

contradictions.reading: The report and the answer are about different things: the Fediverse post describes some flaw in 8.5.12; the PHP security team says it is a separate crash bug of minimal impact, not a way around the RCE fix. The answer came at 09:11 UTC on 22 October, after the vault's copy of the thread (which stops at 22/2), so the site still says PHP has not answered. Open only until the reply is captured; then it should be marked explained and the claim re-graded.

statements.says: PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs
statements.measures: W3Techs' share, credited to W3Techs

statements.who: Tenable, and every other outlet that names W3Techs
statements.says: 69.3% of websites whose server-side language is known
statements.measures: W3Techs' share on the day

statements.who: W3Techs' yearly table, fetched by the desk
statements.says: 75.2% on 1 January 2025; 72.4% on 1 January 2026; 69.3% on 23 October 2026
statements.measures: the same measure over time

contradictions.reading: The same measurer at different dates. Reuters' 75% matches W3Techs' figure for January 2025, not the 69.3% W3Techs showed when Reuters wrote; the attribution is right and the number is out of date. Investigation php-share.
contradictions.settle: Capture W3Techs' yearly table into the vault (board 033).
